porbos.title: The Question From Which the Seerah Begins • The Love Even an Enemy Recognises • Uhud’s Shield, and the Price of Love • Love Is Not Born Without Knowing • This Love Is Not an Extra, It Is a Condition of Faith

blocks.0: The Question From Which the Seerah Begins
blocks.1: Dear reader, we have sat down to read about a man whom our eyes have never seen; and yet, fourteen hundred years on, in millions upon millions of hearts, love stirs the moment his name is mentioned, and a prayer of blessing (durood) upon him comes to the lips. But the first question of this book is not about him. The question is about me. About you.
blocks.2: The people of your home, the old customers at your shop, the stranger who sits beside you on the bus every morning: they watch you every day. Not your words, only your movements. How you get up, how you sit. What your face does when you are angry, what your eyes do when you laugh. How far your hand opens in a transaction, how soft your voice grows in speech. After watching for so long, do they ever sense that deep inside this person there is a profound attachment to someone? That this person loves someone dearly?
blocks.3: We all say, ‘I love the Prophet {{1}}.’ Saying it does not cost even a breath. We say it in gatherings, we sing it on the night of Milad, we say it with eyes wet when naming a child. If anyone voices even the slightest doubt, it is as though we catch fire at once. But however easily the claim comes to the lips, the proof does not come so easily. Love is a thing inside the chest. To bring it outside, to stand it up, to weigh it and show it to others, is no easy matter.
blocks.4: And yet, this very hard proof once opened itself, unasked, before one man. It was fourteen hundred years ago. The man was not a Muslim. He had not come to hear any talk about love. He had come as an envoy of the enemy side, to haggle over the terms of a treaty. For a while he sat quietly. He kept only his two eyes open. And in that short while something caught his notice that he could not help telling his own people when he returned to Makkah.
blocks.5: So let the first lesson of the Seerah begin through the eyes of that unfamiliar man.
blocks.6: The Love Even an Enemy Recognises
blocks.7: The plain of Hudaybiyyah. Bargaining over the terms of a treaty was under way. Several representatives of the Quraysh came to speak with the Prophet {{1}}. One of them was ‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ud, chief of the Thaqif tribe of Ta’if, an old ally of the Quraysh. Arab politics was as familiar to him as the lines of his own palm. Caesar, Chosroes, the Negus: he had seen every court.
blocks.8: He sat before the Prophet {{1}}. He spoke. He argued. And in between, his eyes swept around.
blocks.9: He saw the Prophet {{1}} making ablution, and the Companions not letting even a single drop of that water fall to the ground. As though, if one drop fell, something great would be lost. He saw that the moment the Prophet said a single word, everyone rushed to carry it out. Not one of them asked, even once, why. He saw that when the Prophet spoke, everyone’s voice before him dropped low of its own accord. No one could lift his eyes and keep looking at his face. Such respect, such love.
blocks.10: ‘Urwah stood up. Returning to Makkah, he said to the Quraysh—
blocks.11: “O Quraysh! I have been to the courts of kings. To Caesar, to Chosroes, to the Negus. By Allah, I have not seen any king whom his people honour as the companions of Muhammad honour Muhammad.”{{1}}
blocks.12: The man was not a Muslim. There was no need at all for him to say this. What would he gain by praising an enemy! Yet he said it. Because there was no way for this not to catch the eye.
blocks.13: ‘Urwah was not the only one to see this. It was a few years later. Zayd ibn al-Dathinna, a Companion captured in the Raji‘ expedition, had been brought to Makkah and taken out to be killed. Standing in the crowd was Abu Sufyan, who had not yet accepted Islam. He asked Zayd, “Don’t you wish that Muhammad were in your place today, and that you were sitting safe at home with your family?” Zayd answered—
blocks.14: “By Allah, I would not even like Muhammad {{1}} to have a thorn pricking his foot where he is now, in exchange for my sitting in my own home.”{{2}}
blocks.15: Abu Sufyan then said, “I have never seen anyone love another person as the companions of Muhammad love him.” This is the first sign of love. Love does not have to be announced aloud. It blooms of itself in the walking, in the glance, in the tone of the voice, in the care of the hands. And an outsider, a complete stranger, even an enemy, catches it in a single instant.
blocks.16: Uhud’s Shield, and the Price of Love
blocks.17: ‘Urwah saw it sitting in a quiet gathering. That day the sign of love was caught in good manners, in the tone of the voice, in the lowering of the eyes. But the true measure of love is taken elsewhere. Where a price has to be paid.
blocks.18: The field of Uhud. Arrows flying, the ranks broken, people scattered. The Prophet {{1}} was standing in the open field. A man came running. Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah. An arrow was coming straight toward the Prophet {{2}}. Talha spread out his hand in front of the arrow. That very day the hand was finished. For the rest of his life that hand never moved again.
blocks.20: “I saw Talha’s hand paralysed. On the day of Uhud he shielded the Prophet {{1}} with this very hand.”{{2}}
blocks.21: One hand. Useless for a whole lifetime. In exchange, one arrow that did not touch the beloved. Is this a gain or a loss! What would Talha have said if asked!
blocks.22: There was another man on that field. Abu Talha (RA), the best archer of the Ansar. He took a shield and stood in front of the Prophet {{1}}. He held the shield not over himself but over him. That day two or three bows broke in his hands.
blocks.23: The Prophet {{1}} now and then wanted to raise his head to see the enemy’s position. And each time Abu Talha would tremble—
blocks.24: “May my father and mother be sacrificed for you! Do not raise your head, or some arrow of theirs will strike you. My chest is before your chest.”{{1}}
blocks.25: ‘My chest is before your chest.’ In this one sentence the entire lesson is held. The man is not calculating. He is not arguing. He is not setting conditions. He simply stands, making his body a wall; and he says, if an arrow must come, let it pass through my chest.
blocks.26: Not only on the field: this price of love was being paid in the homes of Madinah too. On the day of Uhud, word came to a woman of the Banu Dinar tribe that her father had been martyred. A little later, word came that her brother too. Then word came that her husband too. Each time she asked only one question: How is the Prophet {{1}}? People said, he is well. Still she was not at peace; she said, show me him once. Seeing the Prophet {{2}} safe and sound from afar, she said—
blocks.27: “As long as you are safe, every calamity is trivial.”{{1}}
blocks.28: What ‘Urwah had seen from the outside opened up from within at Uhud. What love is cannot be understood in the language of gatherings. It is understood at that moment when the price is asked.
blocks.29: Love Is Not Born Without Knowing
blocks.30: These people, who would not let the water of ablution fall to the ground: were they always like this? No.
blocks.31: ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab once set out with a drawn sword to finish off the Prophet {{1}}. Abu Sufyan came against him with an army three times over, at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. At Uhud the blood of Muslims flowed through Khalid’s tactics. ‘Ikrimah was the son of Abu Jahl. Wahshi’s spear pierced the chest of Hamzah (RA). And Hind chewed that liver. These very people. Exactly these became, later, the kind of people ‘Urwah had been speaking of.
blocks.32: How deep this change was can be sensed from a single remark of ‘Amr ibn al-‘As. The man who once rushed to the court of Abyssinia to bring the Companions back said, after accepting Islam—
blocks.33: “No one was dearer to me than the Messenger of Allah {{1}}, and no one was more majestic in my eyes. Out of reverence I could not even fill my eyes with looking at him. If anyone asks me to describe his appearance, I cannot; because I never looked at him with my eyes full.”{{2}}
blocks.34: No magic had happened in between. No spell had been recited. Only one thing had happened: suhbah, companionship. They came to know the man. And what a wonderful rule this is! Whoever has once truly come to know him has never been able to go back.
blocks.35: Here lies the real reason for reading the Seerah. Love cannot be built by scolding. By giving sermons, by shaming, by shouting ‘Love him, love him’; in no way at all. Love is born from just one thing: knowing. How can I love someone I do not know! And how can I help loving someone I have once truly come to know!
blocks.36: This Love Is Not an Extra, It Is a Condition of Faith
blocks.37: Someone might now think that this is merely an added beauty. Nice if you have it, fine if you do not. No, it is not fine. The Prophet {{1}} himself drew the line. He said—
blocks.39: “By the One in whose hand is my soul! None of you will be a believer until I am dearer to him than his father, his children and all of mankind.”{{1}}
blocks.40: This is worth pausing over. More than the father. More than the children. More than all people. A father’s love is the oldest love a person has. A child’s love is the deepest. One must pass beyond these two. And even then it is not the end.

footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions (al-Maghazi), Chapter on the Battle of Uhud, hadith 4063; on the authority of Qays ibn Abi Hazim (RH).
footnotes.3: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions, Chapter on the Battle of Uhud, hadith 4064; on the authority of Anas ibn Malik (RA).
footnotes.4: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (Uhud). A Seerah narration; it is not in the sound hadith collections.
footnotes.5: Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, hadith 121.
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Faith, Chapter: Love of the Messenger {{1}} Is Part of Faith, hadith 15; Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith, hadith 44; on the authority of Anas (RA).

quiz.q: Of which tribe was ‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ud the chief at Hudaybiyyah?
o: The Quraysh of Makkah, as is generally held
The Thaqif of Ta’if
The Ghatafan of Najd
The Khazraj of Madinah
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ud, chief of the Thaqif tribe of Ta’if, an old ally of the Quraysh.’

quiz.q: What behaviour of the Companions did ‘Urwah observe at Hudaybiyyah?
o: They were asking the reason behind the Prophet’s ﷺ commands
They were arguing among themselves over the terms of the treaty
They would not let even a drop of the ablution water fall to the ground
They were preparing their weapons and gear for war
quiz.e: ‘Urwah saw that the Companions ‘did not let even a single drop of that water fall to the ground’, that at a single word everyone rushed to act, and that before the Prophet ﷺ everyone’s voices dropped low.

quiz.q: What did ‘Urwah say to the Quraysh after returning to Makkah?
o: The Companions will never agree to a treaty
Caesar’s subjects obey him more
The Companions obey the Prophet ﷺ only out of fear
People do not honour any king like this
quiz.e: ‘Urwah said that although he had seen the courts of Caesar, Chosroes and the Negus, he had seen no king ‘whom his people honour as the companions of Muhammad honour Muhammad.’

quiz.q: In answer to Abu Sufyan’s question while in captivity, what did Zayd ibn al-Dathinna (RA) say?
o: He did not want even a thorn to prick the Prophet’s ﷺ foot
He would agree to a treaty in exchange for his release
He agreed to be in the Prophet’s ﷺ place
He agreed to return safely to his family at home
quiz.e: Hearing this answer, Abu Sufyan, then a non-Muslim, exclaimed, ‘I have never seen anyone love another as the companions of Muhammad love him.’

quiz.q: ‘Urwah, though not a Muslim, praised the Companions’ love before the Quraysh. What is the significance of this in the lesson?
o: He had secretly accepted Islam
It was so clear that even an enemy’s eye could not miss it
He said it as a diplomatic move
His main aim was to frighten the Quraysh
quiz.e: ‘Urwah had nothing to gain by praising an enemy; ‘yet he said it, because there was no way for this not to catch the eye’. Love shows itself in behaviour.

quiz.q: What became of the hand of Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah (RA) on the day of Uhud?
o: The hand was cut off
The hand became paralysed that very day
The hand received only a slight scratch
The hand received a deep sword wound
quiz.e: He spread out his hand in front of the arrow coming toward the Prophet ﷺ; ‘that very day the hand was finished. For the rest of his life that hand never moved again.’

quiz.q: ‘My chest is before your chest.’ Who was standing with a shield on the field of Uhud saying this?
o: Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah (RA)
Qays ibn Abi Hazim (RH)
Abu Talha al-Ansari (RA)
Anas ibn Malik (RA)
quiz.e: Abu Talha (RA), ‘the best archer of the Ansar’, was shielding the Prophet ﷺ with a shield, and said this each time the Prophet raised his head.

quiz.q: What do ‘Urwah’s testimony and the events of Uhud, taken together, show about love?
o: Both speak only of the manners of gatherings, as is generally held
Love is proved only on the battlefield
In a gathering it shows in good manners; at Uhud, in paying the price
Love is not really something to be proved
quiz.e: ‘Urwah saw it in a quiet gathering, ‘in good manners, in the tone of the voice, in the lowering of the eyes’; but the true measure is taken ‘where a price has to be paid’.

quiz.q: What is the story of the woman of Banu Dinar on the day of Uhud brought in the lesson to show?
o: That women too took part on the battlefield then
That news cannot be believed without verification
That it is better not to show grief even when grieved
That the price of love was being paid in homes as well
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘Not only on the field: this price of love was being paid in the homes of Madinah too’. The woman said, ‘As long as you are safe, every calamity is trivial.’

quiz.q: ‘My chest is before your chest.’ Why does the lesson say that the ‘entire lesson’ is held in this one sentence?
o: It is a picture of shielding him with one’s life, without calculation
It reveals the whole military strategy of Uhud, as is generally held
It is the name of a famous hadith book
It hints at the terms of the treaty
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘The man is not calculating. He is not arguing. He is not setting conditions’; he only makes his body a wall and says, if an arrow must come, let it pass through my chest.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what was the ‘one thing only’ behind the transformation of the former enemies?
o: Long and strict training
Victories in one battle after another
Fear of harsh rule and punishment
Suhbah, that is, coming to know him
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘No magic had happened in between. No spell had been recited. Only one thing had happened: suhbah. They came to know the man.’

quiz.q: After accepting Islam, what would ‘Amr ibn al-‘As (RA) say about the Prophet ﷺ?
o: Out of reverence he could not lift his eyes to him
He would write down every word of the Prophet ﷺ
He had fought the Prophet ﷺ more than anyone
He could see the Prophet ﷺ only from afar
quiz.e: In the narration of Sahih Muslim, ‘Amr (RA) says, ‘No one was dearer to me than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ… Out of reverence I could not even fill my eyes with looking at him.’

quiz.q: ‘How can I love someone I do not know!’ What argument does the lesson build with these words?
o: Love is created only through sermons and scolding
Love comes from knowing, hence the reading of the Seerah
The Seerah is a subject written only for scholars
Love comes by inheritance from lineage
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘Love cannot be built by scolding… Love is born from just one thing: knowing.’ The Seerah is the path to that knowing.

quiz.q: Someone wants to create love of the Prophet ﷺ in others’ hearts by scolding and shaming. According to the lesson, what is wrong with this?
o: Love comes down through generations, not through effort
This is the most effective way of creating love
Instead of scolding, giving rewards alone will do
Love does not come this way; it comes from knowing
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘Love cannot be built by scolding… Love is born from just one thing: knowing’, which is why reading the Seerah is needed.

quiz.q: According to the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, no one can be a believer until he is dearer to that person than…
o: his wealth, his clan and his friends
his father, his children and everyone else
his teacher, his friend and his relatives
his neighbour and his colleague
quiz.e: In the words of the hadith, ‘None of you will be a believer until I am dearer to him than his father, his children and all of mankind.’

quiz.q: Even after passing beyond the love of father and children, where does the measure of love end up?
o: The test of love takes place only in gatherings
Love is complete with the declaration of the mouth alone
The measure rises higher still and lands on one’s life
It is enough for love to be greater than wealth
quiz.e: The lesson says that after passing beyond father and children it is ‘not the end’; in the story of ‘Umar (RA) the measure becomes more than one’s own life.

porbos.title: How ‘Umar (RA) Found the Measure • A Claim Is Cheap; the Proof Is in Following • Beside the One I Love, on the Day of Gathering •A Debt to Him That Can Never Be Repaid • The Five Fruits of Reading the Seerah • Incomparable Even in the Eyes of a Non-Believer

blocks.1: One day the Companions were sitting with the Prophet {{1}}. He was holding ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab’s hand. ‘Umar (RA) said, ‘O Messenger of Allah! You are dearer to me than everything; except my own life.’
blocks.2: This is no small statement. The man who had once set out with a sword in his hand is today saying: dearer than everything in the world. Than children, than wealth, than the clan. Only his own life excepted.
blocks.3: The Prophet {{1}} said, ‘No, ‘Umar. By the One in whose hand is my soul! Not until I am dearer to you even than your own life.’
blocks.4: ‘Umar (RA) was silent for a moment. Just a moment. Then he said, ‘By Allah, now you are dearer to me even than my own life.’ The Prophet {{1}} said, ‘Now it is, ‘Umar.’{{2}}
blocks.5: In a single moment the measure was set. More than one’s own life. If it drops a hair’s breadth below this, it is no longer love; it becomes politeness.
blocks.6: A Claim Is Cheap; the Proof Is in Following
blocks.7: Yet there is a trap here. Claiming love is easy. No one comes to verify. People accept it if you merely say it. Allah, the Exalted, has closed off that trap. He did not accept the claim just like that; He asked for proof.
blocks.9: Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.’{{1}}
blocks.10: The verse is worth noticing. The claim is one person’s, and the proof lies in following another. Someone says he loves Allah; Allah says, then walk the path of My Messenger.
blocks.11: So the test of love is not held in gatherings. The test comes exactly where my wish and his Sunnah stand face to face. The moment I let go of my wish and take his path, in that moment love is proved. The rest of the time it is merely a beautiful feeling.
blocks.12: Beside the One I Love, on the Day of Gathering
blocks.13: What this love can bring, the Prophet {{1}} once told in answer to a question from a villager. The man came and asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, when is the Hour?’ The Prophet {{2}} asked in return, ‘What have you prepared for it?’ The man fell silent. Then he said, ‘Not much. I could not store up many prayers and fasts. Only… I love Allah and His Messenger.’ The Prophet {{3}} said—
blocks.15: “You will be with the one you love.”{{1}}
blocks.16: Anas (RA) later said that after accepting Islam we had never been as happy over any saying as we were over this one. In terms of deeds the Companions are beyond our reach. Yet their greatest source of reassurance was this one sentence. Deeds may be few. It is enough that love is not few. Because on the plain of the Gathering, a person will stand beside the one he used to love.
blocks.17: And here a word of fear is hidden too. ‘Whoever loves someone will be with him.’ This holds the other way as well. Whoever’s picture is largest in my heart today, whom I imitate, whose style I adopt, whose way of speaking I copy, whose talk I speak of all day; on the plain of the Gathering I will be called with him. The question rises once in my own mind: with whom will I be called?
blocks.18: A Debt to Him That Can Never Be Repaid
blocks.19: Love is also born of gratitude. So it is necessary to sit down once and reckon exactly what we have received by holding this man’s hand.
blocks.20: We received the knowledge of the One Allah. A people who used to stretch out their hands to stones, who in trouble used to weep at the roots of trees, learned that the One to be called upon is only One.
blocks.21: We received news of what lies beyond death. Man is no longer groping in the dark. Where we came from, where we are going, what we will be asked to account for; all is known.
blocks.22: We received the rules of worship. The wish to call upon Allah alone is not enough; the method of calling upon Him too, it was he who taught.
blocks.23: We received the boundaries of the lawful and the unlawful. Which earnings are permitted, which relations are permitted, where one must stop; the lines were drawn by his hand.
blocks.24: We received dignity. A daughter was a burden; she became a cause of Paradise. A slave was merchandise; Bilal (RA) became the muadhdhin on the roof of the Ka‘bah. An orphan was helpless; to place a hand on his head became an act of worship.
blocks.25: And we received the hope of intercession. On the plain of Resurrection every prophet will say, ‘Nafsi, nafsi.’ My own concern, my own concern. Only one will say, ‘Ummati, ummati.’ My community, my community.
blocks.26: Because they understood the weight of this debt, the Ansar said an astonishing thing on the day of Hunayn. That day the Prophet {{1}} distributed the spoils among the newly Muslim Quraysh chiefs, and gave nothing to the Ansar, trusting in their faith. The Ansar felt a little hurt. The Prophet {{2}} called them and said, ‘People will return home with camels and goats, and you will return home with the Messenger of Allah {{3}}; are you not content with this?’ The Ansar burst into tears until their beards were wet. They said—
blocks.27: “We are content to have the Messenger of Allah {{1}} as our share.”{{2}}
blocks.28: To receive so many things from one man and still not know him, not love him! What is this but ingratitude!
blocks.29: The Five Fruits of Reading the Seerah
blocks.30: The first fruit of reading the Seerah: knowing is born. And from knowing is born love.
blocks.31: The second fruit: following becomes possible. How shall I follow someone whose life I do not know? To learn the way of prayer, one must see how he prayed. To learn what to do at a moment of anger, one must see what he did at a moment of anger.
blocks.32: The third fruit: consolation. There is no hardship in life of which his life does not hold an example. The pain of being orphaned. The pain of laying a child in the grave. The death of loved ones. Being driven from home. Hunger. Slander. Betrayal. Torture on the body. A person broken under the weight of his own sorrow goes to the Seerah and sees that someone has walked this path before him. The dearest person of all has walked it.
blocks.33: The fourth fruit: the method of calling to faith (da‘wah). How to call people, when in secret and when in the open, what language to use with whom; everything is written in his twenty-three years of work.
blocks.34: The fifth fruit: the blueprint for building society and state. This side is so large that it needs a separate discussion. That is the subject of the next passage.
blocks.35: This is why the Seerah is not merely history. History reports the past. The Seerah shows the path for the present.
blocks.36: Incomparable Even in the Eyes of a Non-Believer
blocks.37: Now do a difficult thing. For a little while, change your eyes. Set aside the eyes of faith. And the eyes of love too. Borrow the eyes of a man who does not accept him as a prophet; who sees him only as a figure in history, as an actor in politics, as a reformer of society. What do we see when we look at him through these eyes?
blocks.38: One man. Age forty. No army, no treasury, no kingdom, no dynasty. No empire standing behind him. In the beginning his followers could be counted on the fingers of the hand. After twenty-three years he closed his eyes.
blocks.39: By then the whole Arabian Peninsula, a land that no one had been able to bring under one banner in a thousand years, had become one. The tribal wars had stopped. Wine, gambling, usury, the burying of daughters, each a habit of a thousand years, were gone within a single generation. And within a hundred years of his death, the people of that desert had raised a civilisation whose borders ran from Spain to Sindh. Where in history is there a second example like this!
blocks.40: Those in politics note one thing in particular. History has seen many successful politicians. But power is such a thing that the hand it comes to changes. The man who used to hide in mountain caves, when he sits on the throne, his way of moving changes, his eating changes, his house changes. In this man’s case that did not happen.
blocks.41: On the day of the conquest of Makkah, all Arabia lay beneath his feet. He entered the city seated on a camel, his head bowed so low that his beard nearly touched the saddle; in humility. Standing before those from whose city he had been driven out, those who had killed his companions, dear to him as children, he said, ‘Go, you are free.’
blocks.42: And until the last day of his life, for month after month no fire was lit in his hearth. At the time of his death his iron coat of mail was pawned to a Jew. Head of a state, yet he left behind not a single dirham as inheritance. With which king can one compare this man!
blocks.43: Sociologists are astonished by another thing. Making laws is easy. Getting laws obeyed is hard. How many reformers of the world have written how many beautiful words, and those words have stayed on paper.
blocks.44: But here the reform was not merely announced; it entered people’s habits. The nation that used to bury its daughters in the ground, the fathers of that very nation learned to sit with a daughter on the lap. In a society where a slave was equal to an animal, the son of a slave became a commander, and another slave climbed to the roof of the Ka‘bah to call the adhan.
blocks.45: And the reform began from his own house. At the Farewell Hajj he declared: all usury of the Jahiliyyah is cancelled; and the first usury I cancel is that of my own uncle. All blood-vengeance is abolished; and the first blood I forgive is that of my own clan. What reformer has ever brought the first blow down on his own family!
blocks.46: This is exactly why even those who deny him stop short before him. In 1978 an American writer named Michael Hart made a list of the hundred most influential people in history. At number one on the list he placed Muhammad {{1}}. As the reason he wrote that he was the only man in history who was supremely successful on both the religious and the worldly side. The man is not a Muslim. He had no need to say this. Do you remember ‘Urwah?
blocks.47: Here, however, a word of caution is needed. In our gatherings many beautiful sayings circulate in the names of non-Muslim thinkers, many of which have no reliable source. In this very lesson we will say that popularity is no proof. That rule applies here too. To prove his stature we have no need of borrowed quotations. The verified events of his life are enough.
blocks.48: So this is where we stand. The Seerah is not a book only for religious people. One who wants to run a state will find here the blueprint for building a state. One who wants to change society will find here the method of reform. One who wants to lead will see here how to keep one’s feet on the ground even with power in hand. And one who simply wants to love will find here that man whom, once you know him, there is no going back.

quiz.q: When exactly did the Prophet ﷺ say, ‘Now it is, ‘Umar’?
o: After ‘Umar (RA) had set out with a sword in his hand
After ‘Umar (RA) excepted his own life
After ‘Umar (RA) called him dearer than life
After ‘Umar (RA) called him dearer than everyone
quiz.e: When ‘Umar (RA) said, ‘Now you are dearer to me even than my own life,’ the Prophet ﷺ said right then, ‘Now it is, ‘Umar.’

quiz.q: Which measure of love does the Prophet’s ﷺ acknowledgement, ‘Now it is, ‘Umar’, establish?
o: It is enough if it is greater than wealth and clan
It is enough if it is greater than children and family
It is enough to declare it repeatedly with the mouth
Greater than one’s own life; otherwise it is mere politeness
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘More than one’s own life. If it drops a hair’s breadth below this, it is no longer love; it becomes politeness.’

quiz.q: Someone wants to test his own love. According to the measure of chapter 6, what must it be like?
o: It is enough if it equals the love of family
It must be greater than wealth and rank
It must be greater even than one’s own life
At least something one declares regularly with the mouth
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘More than one’s own life. If it drops a hair’s breadth below this, it is no longer love; it becomes politeness.’

quiz.q: In verse 31 of Surah Al ‘Imran, what is asked as proof of loving Allah?
o: Much charity and alms
Regular voluntary worship
Declaring love in gatherings
Following the Messenger ﷺ
quiz.e: In the words of the verse, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me’; the claim is one person’s, and the proof lies in following another.

quiz.q: ‘The test of love is not held in gatherings.’ So where, according to the lesson, is the test held?
o: Where wish and Sunnah stand face to face
Where more people speak of love, as is generally held
Where hardship and severe suffering descend
Where Ramadan and the season of worship arrive
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘The moment I let go of my wish and take his path, in that moment love is proved. The rest of the time it is merely a beautiful feeling.’

quiz.q: In daily life, in some matter, one’s own wish and the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ come face to face. According to chapter 7, when is love proved?
o: When one’s own wish is put first
When one lets go of one’s wish and takes his path
When a middle course between the two is chosen
When the decision is put off for later
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘The moment I let go of my wish and take his path, in that moment love is proved.’

quiz.q: On the matter of preparing for the Hour, what did the villager say to the Prophet ﷺ?
o: That he loves Allah and His Messenger
That he had given much charity and performed several Hajjes
That he had stored up many voluntary prayers and fasts
That he prays long night prayers (tahajjud)
quiz.e: He said, ‘I could not store up many prayers and fasts. Only… I love Allah and His Messenger.’ The Prophet ﷺ said, ‘You will be with the one you love.’

quiz.q: One says, ‘My deeds are few, so my hope of salvation is also small.’ In the light of chapter 8, what is the most correct reply?
o: True, without deeds love has no value
Nothing will come without deeds equal to the Companions’
Even mentioning love with the mouth is forbidden
Deeds may be few; love is not few
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘Deeds may be few. It is enough that love is not few’, because on the Day of Gathering a person will be beside the one he used to love.

quiz.q: On intercession, the lesson says that on the plain of Resurrection, although all prophets say ‘Nafsi, nafsi’, one will say…
o: ‘Rabbi, Rabbi’
‘Ummati, ummati’
‘Nafsi, nafsi’
‘Ahad, Ahad’
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, every prophet will think of himself, ‘Only one will say, Ummati, ummati.’

quiz.q: On the day of Hunayn, after the distribution of spoils, what did the Ansar say on hearing the Prophet’s ﷺ words?
o: They asked for their share of the spoils back
They did not object to the distribution among the Quraysh
They were content to have the Messenger of Allah ﷺ
They wanted to return quickly to Madinah
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, people will return with camels and goats, and you will return with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; the Ansar wept and said, ‘We are content to have the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as our share.’ (Sahih al-Bukhari 4330; Sahih Muslim 1061)

quiz.q: ‘A debt to him’: by raising this debt, to which source of love does the lesson point?
o: Love born of fear
Love born of gratitude
Love born of habit
Love born of shame before people
quiz.e: The lesson begins, ‘Love is also born of gratitude’, then goes through the knowledge of the One Allah (Tawhid), news of the Hereafter, the rules of worship, the lawful and the unlawful, dignity and intercession.

quiz.q: To receive so much from the Prophet ﷺ and yet not know him, not love him: what does the lesson call this?
o: A natural neglect
A great ingratitude
A minor flaw only
Merely a lack of knowledge
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘To receive so many things from one man and still not know him, not love him! What is this but ingratitude!’

quiz.q: In what order are the five fruits of reading the Seerah arranged according to the lesson?
o: Consolation, knowing, following, da‘wah, state blueprint
Knowing, consolation, following, state blueprint, da‘wah
Following, knowing, da‘wah, consolation, state blueprint
Knowing, following, consolation, da‘wah, state blueprint
quiz.e: In the lesson the fruits come in this order: first knowing (and love from it), second following, third consolation, fourth the method of da‘wah, fifth the blueprint for building society and state.

quiz.q: The lesson says ‘the Seerah is not merely history’; what reason is given?
o: History lies, the Seerah tells the truth
The Seerah contains only accounts of wars, as is generally held
History tells of the past, the Seerah shows the way
History and Seerah are two names for the same subject
quiz.e: After the five fruits, the lesson concludes, ‘History reports the past. The Seerah shows the path for the present.’

quiz.q: According to the lesson, what will a person broken by sorrow find in the Seerah?
o: Consolation, an example of hardship in his life
A perfect method of giving da‘wah
A complete blueprint for running a state
Merely a long account of past events
quiz.e: The third fruit is consolation: ‘There is no hardship in life of which his life does not hold an example’; the broken person sees that the dearest person too walked this path.

quiz.q: Where did Michael Hart place the Prophet ﷺ in his 1978 list of ‘the hundred most influential people’?
o: At number one on the list
At number three
At number ten
At the very end of the list
quiz.e: Hart places the Prophet ﷺ at ‘number one’, writing as the reason that he was the only man in history who was supremely successful on both the religious and the worldly side.

quiz.q: At the Farewell Hajj, which usury did the Prophet ﷺ cancel first?
o: Usury owed to a Jew
The usury of his own uncle
The usury of Abu Jahl’s family
The usury of a tribe of Madinah
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘the first usury I cancel is that of my own uncle’; and the first blood forgiven was that of his own clan.

quiz.q: What is the astonishment of sociologists about the Prophet’s ﷺ social reform, as mentioned in the lesson?
o: He left behind many beautiful laws
His reform needed outside help
His reform remained only on paper
The reform did not remain a declaration; it entered habits
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘here the reform was not merely announced; it entered people’s habits’, and it ‘began from his own house’.

quiz.q: On the quotations of non-Muslim thinkers, with which principle does the lesson’s caution agree?
o: Popularity is no proof; verifying is enough
Any famous quotation is enough as proof
No statement of non-Muslims can be accepted
Only Michael Hart’s quotation can be used
quiz.e: The lesson says, ‘To prove his stature we have no need of borrowed quotations. The verified events of his life are enough’, which is the application of the principle ‘popularity is no proof’.

quiz.q: Someone said, ‘To prove the Prophet’s ﷺ stature we need to collect the quotations of famous Western thinkers.’ What is the lesson’s reply?
o: Yes, the more quotations collected, the better
Only Michael Hart’s quotation is enough
No, his verified events are enough
Quotations of non-Muslims are not to be used at all
quiz.e: The lesson reminds us to set aside beautiful but unsourced quotations; ‘To prove his stature we have no need of borrowed quotations.’

quiz.q: A ruler or reformer is seeking an ideal of leadership. According to the lesson, what can the Seerah give him?
o: Only the rules of religious rituals
Only the names and lists of past kings
Only various military strategies for winning wars
An example of keeping one’s feet on the ground even with power
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘The Seerah is not a book only for religious people’; one who wants to lead ‘will see here how to keep one’s feet on the ground even with power in hand’.

porbos.title: The Sources of the Seerah and Their Order of Rank • Four Measures for Verifying a Report • Fame and Authenticity Are Not the Same • What the Qur’an Says • Finally: Our Five Duties • The Last Word

blocks.0: The Sources of the Seerah and Their Order of Rank
blocks.1: Now let me pause and speak of practical matters. When we sit down to read the Seerah, which book will we read from, and how much of each report will we accept? This much must be known at the very start.
blocks.2: The first and highest source of the Seerah is the Noble Qur’an. Badr, Uhud, the Trench, Hudaybiyyah, the Ifk (the slander), Tabuk; the account of these events was given by Allah Himself. What has come in the Qur’an has no testimony above it.
blocks.3: The second source is the books of hadith: Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud, Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, Sunan al-Nasa’i, Sunan Ibn Majah, Musnad Ahmad.
blocks.4: The third source is the Maghazi and the early Seerah works: the Seerah of Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Hisham, al-Waqidi’s Kitab al-Maghazi, and Ibn Sa‘d’s al-Tabaqat al-Kubra.
blocks.5: The fourth source is the compilations of later periods: Ibn Kathir’s al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, Ibn al-Qayyim’s Zad al-Ma‘ad, and Qadi ‘Iyad’s al-Shifa’.
blocks.6: These works are not equal in rank. The Qur’an and the sound (sahih) hadith stand above all. The Maghazi works hold many valuable accounts, but weak reports have crept in there too. So nothing can be accepted without verification.
blocks.7: Four Measures for Verifying a Report
blocks.8: Reports of hadith and events fall mainly into four levels.
blocks.9: Sahih (sound): one whose chain is unbroken, whose narrators are upright and of full memory, and which has no defect or contradiction.
blocks.10: Hasan (good): one that fulfils all the conditions of the sahih, except that a narrator’s memory is somewhat weaker. This too is admissible as evidence.
blocks.11: Da‘if (weak): one with a weakness in the chain or in a narrator. In matters of creed and rulings on the lawful and the unlawful it is not evidence. In matters of virtues and encouragement it may be used with conditions, provided the weakness is not severe and it does not contradict any sound principle.
blocks.12: Mawdu‘ (fabricated): invented. This is outright falsehood attributed to the Prophet {{1}}. There is no room for its use. As for one who knowingly tells a lie in his name, his abode is Hell; this warning is his own.
blocks.13: Fame and Authenticity Are Not the Same
blocks.14: Here lies a great danger. If we are not wary of it, what gets read is stories in the name of the Seerah. Many of the tales that circulate most in gatherings have no foundation at all. The more beautiful a tale, the more it brings tears to the eyes, the faster it spreads. As it spreads, people eventually think: since so many people are saying it, surely it is true.
blocks.15: But fame is no proof. Telling a report in a thousand gatherings does not make its chain strong. And it must be remembered that the true biography of the Prophet {{1}} is so rich that there is no need at all for invented events. What is true is enough. The fabricated word added in an effort to raise his honour does not raise it; it spreads falsehood in his name.
blocks.16: So the rule of this book is only one. What has been verified will be written. What has not been verified will be left out; or else it will be said plainly that its basis is weak.
blocks.18: Through the events of the Seerah and through the hadith, we have found the same point again and again so far: the real form of love is following. That very note is clearer still in the Qur’an. The pillars of this whole discussion Allah Himself has fastened in four verses. The first verse joins proof to the claim. Not the word of the mouth; love is recognised in following.
blocks.20: (O Prophet,) say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; then Allah too will love you and forgive you your sins.’ And Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.{{1}}
blocks.21: Following whom? The second verse tells us: the model has been set in the life of the Messenger himself. The urge to read the Seerah comes from here.
blocks.23: Certainly for you, in the Messenger of Allah, there is an excellent example, for those who hope in Allah and the Last Day and remember Allah much.{{1}}
blocks.24: An everyday expression of love for that life is durood, the prayer of blessing upon him. In the third verse, what Allah Himself and His angels do, the believer too is told to do.
blocks.26: Surely Allah and His angels send durood upon the Prophet. O believers, you too send durood upon him and offer salutations of peace in the proper manner.{{1}}
blocks.27: And where the weight of love must finally rest is stated sternly in the fourth verse. If, above father, child, wealth, business, everything, Allah, His Messenger and His path are not dear, then one must wait for Allah’s decree.
blocks.29: (O Prophet,) say, ‘If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, your clan, the wealth you have earned, the trade whose slackening you fear, and the dwellings you like are dearer to you than Allah, His Messenger and striving in His way, then wait until Allah brings His decree.’ And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.{{1}}
blocks.30: Read together, the four verses make the picture clear: the proof of love is in following; the model for following is in his life; one part of fulfilling his right is durood; and above all other loves is the place of love for him. Keeping this note in mind, let us now come to the last word: what exactly are our duties toward the Prophet {{1}}.
blocks.32: All told, our duties toward the Prophet {{1}} are five.
blocks.33: One, faith (iman). To fix firmly in the heart the belief that he is the last Messenger sent by Allah. Leaving him aside, not a single path of guidance is open.
blocks.34: Two, love (muhabbah). Love beyond father and child and all people, beyond one’s own life.
blocks.35: Three, obedience and following (ittiba‘). Obeying his commands, keeping away from what he forbade, drawing his habits into one’s own life.
blocks.36: Four, durood and salam. What Allah Himself and His angels do, the believer is commanded to do as well.
blocks.37: Five, conveying his religion. The message he brought to us with his life will not stop with us alone.
blocks.38: The first is of the heart. The last is of society. The middle three are of daily life. And the first step of this whole path is knowing him. So reading the Seerah is no hobby. It is the first instalment of love.
blocks.40: ‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ud heard no speech that day. No one sat him down and called him to the faith. He simply sat for a while with his eyes open. And in that he saw something he could not help but tell on returning to Makkah.
blocks.41: So the question turns and comes back to us. The people of my house, the customers in my shop, the fellow passenger beside me on the bus; they see me every day. Do they see in the way I move something that makes them realise: this person loves someone dearly?
blocks.42: ‘Urwah, though an outsider, caught it. If those closest to me cannot catch it, then where is the love, really! In the heart, or only on the tongue?

43.title: Practical Resolve
43.text: ‘Urwah, though an outsider, sensed the love of the Companions by watching their conduct.

blocks.44: Today I will ask myself one question: seeing my conduct, would anyone realise that I love him?
blocks.45: Today I will settle on one small practice of the Sunnah, which from today on I will not give up.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, which is the ‘first and highest source’ of the Seerah?
o: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim
The Seerah work of Ibn Hisham
The Noble Qur’an and its account
Ibn Kathir’s al-Bidayah
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘The first and highest source of the Seerah is the Noble Qur’an… What has come in the Qur’an has no testimony above it.’

quiz.q: An account in a Maghazi work conflicts with an account in Sahih al-Bukhari. Which one is given priority in the lesson’s framework?
o: The Maghazi account, because it has more detail
The sound hadith, because its place is above all
The account more commonly circulated in gatherings
Both are equal; either may be taken
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘These works are not equal in rank. The Qur’an and the sound hadith stand above all’; weak reports have crept into the Maghazi too, so nothing is accepted without verification.

quiz.q: Among the four levels of reports, which is called ‘fabricated’, with no room for its use?
o: Da‘if
Hasan
Sahih
Mawdu‘
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘Mawdu‘: fabricated. This is outright falsehood attributed to the Prophet ﷺ. There is no room for its use.’

quiz.q: What is the lesson’s position on a weak (da‘if) report?
o: In matters of creed and the lawful and unlawful it is evidence too
It is not evidence in rulings, but may be used in virtues
In terms of chain it has equal rank with the sahih
Like the mawdu‘, there is no room for its use
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘In matters of creed and rulings on the lawful and the unlawful it is not evidence. In matters of virtues and encouragement it may be used with conditions’, provided the weakness is not severe and it does not contradict a sound principle.

quiz.q: Someone sits down to read the Seerah and decides to learn it only from the stories of popular sermon books. What is the lesson’s advice?
o: First to learn the order of the sources and the rules of verification
That is enough; no separate verification is needed
It is better to read only hadith and not the Seerah
The Seerah must be read from Arabic books alone
quiz.e: The parts on ‘which book to read from’ and the ‘four measures for verifying a report’ say that the rank of the sources and the difference between sahih, hasan, da‘if and mawdu‘ must be known at the very start; otherwise ‘what gets read is stories in the name of the Seerah’.

quiz.q: A preacher is telling a heart-touching but unsourced tale. According to the lesson’s principle, what should the listener do?
o: Not to tell it in the Prophet’s name until it is verified
Since many tell it, to assume it true and spread it
Because the tale is beautiful, to accept it without verification
To spread the tale further with more colour added
quiz.e: The lesson’s rule: ‘fame is no proof’; ‘what has been verified will be written’, and if it is not verified, it must be said plainly that its basis is weak.

quiz.q: When the four verses of the part ‘What the Qur’an Says’ are read together, which picture becomes clear according to the lesson?
o: Love is only of the heart, nothing outward
Love is proved only on the battlefield
Proof in following, model in his life, right in durood
Love is complete in a declaration with the mouth
quiz.e: The lesson’s conclusion: ‘the proof of love is in following; the model for following is in his life; one part of fulfilling his right is durood; and above all other loves is the place of love for him.’

quiz.q: Which five duties toward the Prophet ﷺ does the lesson name?
o: Faith, love, following, durood and conveying the message
Faith, prayer, fasting, zakah and sacrifice
Love, Milad, Qiyam, Na‘t and gatherings, as is generally held
Prayer, fasting, charity, supplication and recitation
quiz.e: The lesson’s list: faith, love, obedience and following, durood and salam, and conveying his religion.

quiz.q: How does the lesson hint that the ‘five duties’ can be divided?
o: All of them are works purely within the heart
The first three are of society, the last two of the heart
The first is of the heart, the last of society
All of them relate only to Ramadan
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘The first is of the heart. The last is of society. The middle three are of daily life.’

quiz.q: At both the beginning and the end of the lesson, a question is turned toward the reader; what is its closest meaning?
o: How much of the Seerah have I managed to memorise? as is generally held
How many times a year have I managed to go to a Milad?
How many Seerah books have I read so far?
Seeing my conduct, does anyone understand my love?
quiz.e: In the lesson’s words, ‘If those closest to me cannot catch it, then where is the love, really! In the heart, or only on the tongue?’
